chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
title: Public radio and television and their licenses
summary: Herman wants educators to organise to push public TV and radio, saying broadcasters treat public airwaves as personal property.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But I think that's where it should be headed. And I think if all the groupings who would get together every year and discuss all this, including the jazz band programs
and whatever, it should be concentrating on that part of the effort. How do we allow our youth and our people who have all this ability, how do we allow them to exploit it?

I would start with public television, public radio. And then I would get into the more sensitive areas, because we can make them lose their licenses. Do you realize that? Do you want to hear an old man get hot?
Because I know that it's out there and I know it's available.

Except who (unintelligible) has enough energy nor time to put up with all this crap. But, really, what we have to prove is that television has not done the job, radio above all has done the worst job, that you can with a public thing, they don't own the airwaves. They're selling it like it was their own personal property.
And I'm not an agitator, but I'm an agitator when it gets beyond all hope.

I read, like, editorials by Fred Friendly and a million other people who are very well informed on television and everything that's been around the last 30, 40 years. And they realize we're headed for a big drop. The whole enter-
tainment scene, and it's because they're not allowing anything to surface other than what they dictate.
